blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site against the official GATE 2027 CS syllabus from IIT Madras. The questions are original and in the style of GATE: they drill the concepts GATE repeats, they are not copies of past papers. If the official syllabus changes, the official PDF wins.

### Notation

| Notation | Meaning | Intuition |
|---|---|---|
| f = O(g) | f ≤ c·g for large n | upper bound |
| f = Ω(g) | f ≥ c·g for large n | lower bound |
| f = Θ(g) | both O(g) and Ω(g) | tight bound |
| f = o(g) | f/g → 0 | strictly smaller |
| f = ω(g) | f/g → ∞ | strictly bigger |

If f = O(g) **and** g = O(f), then f = Θ(g). Worst-case, best-case and average-case are different functions of n; GATE asks for the **worst case** unless it says otherwise.

### Order of growth

log log n < log n < (log n)ᵏ < n^ε < n < n log n < n² < n³ < nᵏ < 2ⁿ < n! < nⁿ.

Useful comparisons: **n^(log n) = 2^(log² n)**, which beats any polynomial but loses to 2ⁿ. **(log n)^(log n) = 2^(log n · log log n)** also beats every polynomial and loses to 2^(√n). To compare two functions, take logarithms of both.

### Solving recurrences

| Recurrence | Solution |
|---|---|
| T(n) = T(n − 1) + 1 | Θ(n) |
| T(n) = T(n − 1) + n | Θ(n²). T(n) = n(n + 1)/2 when T(1) = 1 |
| T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 | Θ(2ⁿ). T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1 when T(0) = 0 |
| T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 | Θ(log n) |
| T(n) = T(n/2) + n | Θ(n) |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1 | Θ(n) |
| T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n | Θ(n log n) |
| T(n) = T(√n) + 1 | Θ(log log n) |

**Master theorem.** For T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n) with a ≥ 1, b > 1, compare f(n) with n^(log_b a):

1. If f(n) = O(n^(log_b a − ε)), then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)). *The leaves dominate.*
2. If f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · logᵏ n), then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) · log^(k+1) n). *Every level costs the same.*
3. If f(n) = Ω(n^(log_b a + ε)) (and a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n)), then T(n) = Θ(f(n)). *The root dominates.*

| T(n) | n^(log_b a) | Case | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8T(n/2) + n² | n³ | 1 | Θ(n³) |
| 4T(n/2) + n² | n² | 2 (k = 0) | Θ(n² log n) |
| 3T(n/2) + n | n^1.585 | 1 | Θ(n^(log₂ 3)) |
| 2T(n/2) + n log n | n | 2 (k = 1) | Θ(n log² n) |
| 2T(n/2) + n² | n | 3 | Θ(n²) |
| 7T(n/2) + n² (Strassen) | n^2.81 | 1 | Θ(n^(log₂ 7)) |

### Loop analysis

blocks.title: Counting loop iterations

blocks.text: **Amortised analysis.** A dynamic array that doubles when full copies 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n elements over n appends, so each append costs O(1) amortised. Appending 16 elements, starting from capacity 1, copies 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 elements in all.

- **Compare by logs:** log(n^(log n)) = log² n versus log(2ⁿ) = n, so 2ⁿ wins easily.
- **Master theorem in three lines:** compute n^(log_b a), compare to f(n), and pick the bigger one (or add a log if they tie).
- **Substitute small n** into a recurrence to confirm a closed form such as T(10) = 55 for T(n) = T(n − 1) + n.
- **Nested loops:** when the inner bound depends on the outer variable, write the sum, don't multiply the bounds.
- **A halving loop runs ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 times.**
- **O(g) and Ω(g) together mean Θ(g).** O alone is only an upper bound, so n = O(n²) is true.
blocks.title: Asymptotics cheat codes

blocks.text:
### Searching

- **Linear search:** Θ(n) comparisons in the worst case.
- **Binary search** on a sorted array: at most **⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1** comparisons. For n = 1000 that is 10.

### Sorting

| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Space | Stable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | n | n² | n² | 1 | yes |
| Selection | n² | n² | n² | 1 | no |
| Insertion | n | n² | n² | 1 | yes |
| Merge | n log n | n log n | n log n | n | yes |
| Quick | n log n | n log n | **n²** | log n | no |
| Heap | n log n | n log n | n log n | 1 | no |
| Counting | n + k | n + k | n + k | n + k | yes |
| Radix | d(n + b) | d(n + b) | d(n + b) | n + b | yes |

- **Inversions:** the number of pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]. Insertion sort does exactly as many swaps as there are inversions, so its time is Θ(n + inversions). The array 5, 2, 4, 1, 3 has 7 inversions. Merge sort counts inversions in O(n log n).
- **Quick sort** with the first or last element as pivot degrades to its worst case, n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, on an already sorted array.
- **Merge sort worst case:** T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n − 1, which for n = 8 gives 17 comparisons.
- **Lower bound for comparison sorting:** a decision tree has n! leaves and height at least ⌈log₂ n!⌉ = Θ(n log n). Sorting 5 elements needs at least ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7 comparisons.
- **Counting sort** takes Θ(n + k) for keys in 0…k − 1. **Radix sort** with base b and d digits takes Θ(d(n + b)); n integers below n² sorted in base n need 2 passes, i.e. Θ(n).

### Selection problems

| Task | Comparisons |
|---|---|
| Find the maximum of n | n − 1 |
| Merge two sorted lists of sizes m and n (worst case) | m + n − 1 |
| Maximum and minimum together | ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 (pair up the elements) |
| Second largest (tournament) | n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2 |
| k-th smallest | Θ(n) on average (quickselect); median of medians gives Θ(n) in the worst case |

### Hashing

A hash function h maps keys into m slots. The **load factor** is α = n/m.

- **Chaining:** each slot has a list. An unsuccessful search examines α keys on average, so costs 1 + α; with n = 2000 keys in m = 500 slots the average chain has 4 keys.
- **Open addressing** stores everything in the table and probes a sequence of slots. α < 1. With uniform hashing an unsuccessful search takes about **1/(1 − α)** probes (2 at α = 0.5).
- **Linear probing** (h(k) + i) suffers **primary clustering**; quadratic probing suffers milder secondary clustering; double hashing (h₁(k) + i·h₂(k)) avoids both.
- **Deleting** from an open-addressed table must leave a *tombstone*. Simply emptying the slot breaks later searches that probe through it.
- The probability that 3 keys hashed uniformly into 10 slots land in different slots is (10·9·8)/10³ = 0.72.

blocks.text:
- **Stable sorts:** bubble, insertion, merge, counting, radix. **Not stable:** selection, quick, heap.
- **Already sorted input:** insertion sort O(n), quick sort (first pivot) O(n²), merge sort O(n log n).
- **Comparison counts:** max n − 1, merge m + n − 1, min and max ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2, second largest n + ⌈log n⌉ − 2.
- **Hash tables:** chaining → α, open addressing → 1/(1 − α). Simulate the probe sequence by hand and write the table after each insert.
- **Binary search** is only valid on sorted data. Its worst case is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1.
blocks.title: Sorting and hashing cheat codes

blocks.text:
**Divide** the problem into smaller instances, **conquer** them recursively, **combine** the answers. The running time follows from the recurrence.

| Algorithm | Recurrence | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Binary search | T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 | Θ(log n) |
| Merge sort | T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n | Θ(n log n) |
| Quick sort (balanced split) | T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n | Θ(n log n) |
| Maximum subarray | T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n | Θ(n log n) |
| Closest pair of points | T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n | Θ(n log n) |
| Karatsuba multiplication | T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n | Θ(n^1.585) |
| Strassen matrix multiplication | T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n² | Θ(n^2.81) |
| Counting inversions | merge-sort based | Θ(n log n) |

Merge sort uses Θ(n) extra space for merging, while quick sort uses Θ(log n) stack space on average (Θ(n) in the worst case).

- **Count the subproblems and their size:** a subproblems of size n/b with combine cost f(n). Then use the master theorem.
- **Fewer multiplications win:** Karatsuba uses 3 instead of 4 half-size products, and Strassen 7 instead of 8.
- **Combine step cost decides:** linear combine → n log n, constant combine → n.
blocks.title: Divide-and-conquer cheat codes

blocks.text:
A greedy algorithm makes the best local choice at each step and never reconsiders. It is correct only when the problem has the **greedy-choice property** and **optimal substructure**.

| Problem | Greedy rule | Correct? |
|---|---|---|
| Activity selection (maximise the number of compatible intervals) | pick the earliest **finish** time | yes |
| Fractional knapsack | highest value/weight ratio first | yes |
| **0/1 knapsack** | highest ratio first | **no** (use DP) |
| Huffman coding | repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency nodes | yes |
| Job sequencing with deadlines | highest profit first, placed in the latest free slot ≤ deadline | yes |
| Optimal merge of files | merge the two smallest each time | yes |
| Minimum spanning tree | Kruskal and Prim | yes |
| Single-source shortest paths (non-negative weights) | Dijkstra | yes |
| Coin change | largest coin first | only for canonical systems |

**Worked examples**

- *Activities* (1,3), (2,5), (4,7), (6,9), (8,10), (9,12): by earliest finish pick (1,3), (4,7), (8,10): **3** activities.
- *Huffman* frequencies 3, 5, 7, 9, 12: merge 3 + 5 = 8, then 7 + 8 = 15, then 9 + 12 = 21, then 15 + 21 = 36. The cost (sum of merged weights) is 8 + 15 + 21 + 36 = **80**. For Fibonacci-like frequencies 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 the tree is a chain, and the rarest symbols get codes of length 5.
- *Fractional knapsack*, capacity 40, (value, weight): (30,5), (40,10), (45,15), (60,20). The ratios are 6, 4, 3, 3. Take the first three whole (weight 30, value 115), then 10 of the 20 units of the last item for 30, total **145**. The 0/1 optimum for the same items is only 135.
- *Job sequencing* (profit, deadline): (50,2), (10,1), (20,2), (30,1), (40,3). Take 50 in slot 2, 40 in slot 3, 30 in slot 1, and the other two do not fit: profit **120**.
- *Optimal merge* of file sizes 2, 3, 5, 7: 2 + 3 = 5, 5 + 5 = 10, 7 + 10 = 17. Total cost 5 + 10 + 17 = **32**.
- *Coin change* with coins {1, 3, 4} for 6: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) but the optimum is 3 + 3 (2 coins).

- **Sort by the right key:** finish time for activities, ratio for fractional knapsack, profit for jobs, frequency for Huffman.
- **Huffman cost** = sum of all internal node weights = Σ frequency × code length.
- **Two-minimum merge** (Huffman, optimal merge) uses a heap. The cost is O(n log n).
- **A greedy rule that is not obviously right is usually wrong.** Hunt for a small counterexample, as the coin system {1, 3, 4} gives.
- **A tie in Huffman** can give different trees, but the same total cost.
blocks.title: Greedy cheat codes

blocks.text:
Use DP when a problem has **optimal substructure** and **overlapping subproblems**. Memoisation fills the table top-down from recursion. Tabulation fills it bottom-up. Both turn an exponential recursion into a polynomial one.

| Problem | Recurrence idea | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Fibonacci | F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2) | O(n) |
| 0/1 knapsack | best[c] = max(best[c], best[c − w] + v) | O(nW) |
| Longest common subsequence (LCS) | equal chars: 1 + L[i−1][j−1], else max(L[i−1][j], L[i][j−1]) | O(mn) |
| Edit distance | min(insert, delete, replace) on a table | O(mn) |
| Matrix chain multiplication | min over splits k of m[i][k] + m[k+1][j] + p[i−1]p[k]p[j] | O(n³) |
| Longest increasing subsequence | L[i] = 1 + max L[j] for a[j] < a[i] | O(n²), or O(n log n) |
| Coin change (ways) | ways[x] += ways[x − c] for each coin | O(n·amount) |
| Floyd–Warshall | d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]) | O(V³) |
| Grid paths (right/down) | paths[i][j] = paths[i−1][j] + paths[i][j−1] | O(mn); C(m+n, n) |

**Worked results**

- LCS of ACGTTGCA and CTGACTA has length **5**.
- Edit distance between *algorithm* and *altruistic* is **6**.
- Matrix chain with dimensions 10×20, 20×5, 5×30, 30×8 (p = 10, 20, 5, 30, 8): minimum **2600** scalar multiplications.
- The number of full parenthesisations of a product of n matrices is the Catalan number C(n−1): 42 for n = 6.
- 0/1 knapsack, capacity 40, (weight, value): (5,30), (10,40), (15,45), (20,60): optimum **135**, taking weights 5 + 15 + 20.
- Longest increasing subsequence of 3, 10, 2, 1, 20, 4, 6, 12: length **4** (for example 2, 4, 6, 12).
- Ways to make 10 from coins {1, 2, 5}: **10**. A 5×5 grid of cells has C(8, 4) = **70** monotone paths.

- **Define the state first,** in words: "L[i][j] = LCS length of the first i and first j characters".
- **Table size = time:** (m+1)(n+1) cells with O(1) work per cell is Θ(mn).
- **0/1 knapsack is pseudo-polynomial:** O(nW) depends on the value of W, not on its bit length.
- **Iterate capacity downwards** in the 1-D knapsack array to use each item once. Iterate upwards to allow repeated items (unbounded).
- **Matrix chain:** count the cost p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j] of the final multiplication, and fill the table by increasing chain length.
- **LIS and LCS are different:** LIS needs the inner loop over earlier elements.
blocks.title: DP cheat codes

blocks.text:
### Traversals and their uses

BFS and DFS both take **O(V + E)** with adjacency lists. BFS gives shortest paths in **unweighted** graphs. DFS gives:

- **Edge classification:** tree, back, forward and cross edges. A directed graph has a **cycle exactly when DFS finds a back edge**.
- **Topological sort** of a DAG: vertices in decreasing finish time.
- **Strongly connected components** in O(V + E) with Kosaraju's or Tarjan's algorithm. The directed graph with edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, 3→4, 4→5, 5→4 has 2 SCCs: {1, 2, 3} and {4, 5}.

### Minimum spanning trees

A spanning tree has V − 1 edges. The **cut property** (the lightest edge crossing any cut belongs to some MST) and the **cycle property** (the heaviest edge on a cycle is not in the MST, if unique) justify both algorithms.

| Algorithm | Method | Time |
|---|---|---|
| **Kruskal** | sort edges, add each if it joins two different components (union–find) | O(E log E) = O(E log V) |
| **Prim** | grow one tree, adding the cheapest edge leaving it | O(V²) with an array and a matrix; O(E log V) with a binary heap |

- If all edge weights are **distinct**, the MST is **unique**. Equal weights can give several MSTs, but they all have the same total weight.
- Kruskal on edges AB4, AC2, BC1, BD5, CD8, CE10, DE2, DF6, EF3 (6 vertices) picks BC1, AC2, DE2, EF3 and BD5 for a total of **13**.
- The MST depends only on the *order* of the weights, so replacing every weight w by w² (all positive) leaves the MST unchanged, though the total weight changes.

### Shortest paths

| Algorithm | Handles | Time |
|---|---|---|
| **Dijkstra** | non-negative weights | O((V + E) log V) with a heap; O(V²) with an array |
| **Bellman–Ford** | negative weights, detects negative cycles | O(VE); V − 1 passes of relaxing all edges |
| Shortest path in a DAG | any weights | O(V + E) in topological order |
| **Floyd–Warshall** | all pairs, negative edges (no negative cycles) | O(V³) (about 10⁶ steps for V = 100) |
| BFS | unweighted | O(V + E) |

**Dijkstra fails with negative edges** because it finalises a vertex's distance when it is popped. Worked example: edges S→A 4, S→B 1, B→A 2, A→C 1, B→C 5. Dijkstra finalises B (1), then A (3), then C (4).

- **Kruskal by hand:** sort, then write which component each endpoint is in. Skip an edge if both are in the same one.
- **Prim by hand:** keep a "cheapest edge into the tree" label on each outside vertex and update it as the tree grows.
- **MST edge count** is V − 1. If you picked fewer, the graph is disconnected.
- **Dijkstra by hand:** a table of tentative distances, finalising the smallest each round.
- **Negative edge weights?** Use Bellman–Ford (single source) or Floyd–Warshall (all pairs). Dijkstra may give a wrong answer.
- **Dense graph** (E ≈ V²) → Prim with a matrix, O(V²), is as good as any.

sections.title: Beyond the listed topics: P and NP in one page

blocks.text:
The 2027 syllabus names only complexity analysis, but P and NP questions have appeared in the past, so know the basics.

- **P:** problems solvable in polynomial time. **NP:** problems whose solutions can be *verified* in polynomial time. P ⊆ NP, and whether P = NP is open.
- **NP-hard:** at least as hard as every problem in NP. **NP-complete:** in NP and NP-hard. If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP.
- Known NP-complete: SAT, 3-SAT, clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, subset sum, 0/1 knapsack (decision form), graph colouring (3 colours), travelling salesman (decision form).
- In P: shortest path, MST, 2-SAT, matching, linear programming, primality testing.

| Master theorem | compare f(n) with n^(log_b a) |
| 2T(n/2) + n | Θ(n log n); T(n−1) + n → Θ(n²); T(√n) + 1 → Θ(log log n) |
| Binary search | ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons |

| Merge m and n | m + n − 1 |
| Min and max together | ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2 |
| Chaining / open addressing | α / 1/(1 − α) |
| Activity selection | earliest finish |
| Huffman cost | sum of internal node weights |
| 0/1 knapsack, LCS, edit distance, MCM | O(nW), O(mn), O(mn), O(n³) |
| Kruskal / Prim | O(E log V) / O(V²) or O(E log V) |
| Dijkstra / Bellman–Ford / Floyd–Warshall | O((V+E) log V) / O(VE) / O(V³) |

60 original GATE-style questions on 7 areas. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people. The marks shown are what a question like this would carry in GATE; in the real exam a wrong 1-mark MCQ costs 1/3 mark and a wrong 2-mark MCQ costs 2/3.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Consider f1(n) = n log n, f2(n) = (log n)^(log n), f3(n) = n² and f4(n) = 2^(√n). The correct order of these functions by asymptotic growth, from slowest to fastest, is
items.w: Compare logarithms: log f1 ≈ log n, log f3 = 2 log n, log f2 = log n · log log n (which beats any constant multiple of log n), and log f4 = √n (which beats log n · log log n). So f1 < f3 < f2 < f4.

items.q: *(1 mark)* The solution of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, with T(1) = 1, is
items.w: Here n^(log₂ 2) = n matches f(n) = n exactly, so every level of the recursion tree costs n and there are log n levels: Θ(n log n).

items.q: *(2 marks)* The solution of T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² is
items.w: n^(log₂ 4) = n² equals f(n), so case 2 of the master theorem applies and T(n) = Θ(n² log n).

items.q: *(2 marks)* The solution of T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n² is
items.w: n^(log₂ 8) = n³ grows faster than f(n) = n², so the leaves dominate (case 1): T(n) = Θ(n³).

items.q: *(2 marks)* T(n) = T(n − 1) + n for n ≥ 2, with T(1) = 1. The value of T(10) is
*(2 marks)* T(n) = 2T(n − 1) + 1 for n ≥ 1, with T(0) = 0. The value of T(10) is
items.w: T(n) = 2ⁿ − 1 (the Tower of Hanoi recurrence): T(1) = 1, T(2) = 3, T(3) = 7, … T(10) = 1023.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The solution of T(n) = T(√n) + 1, with T(2) = 1, is
items.w: Each step squares-roots n, so after k steps the argument is n^(1/2ᵏ). The recursion stops when 2ᵏ ≈ log n, i.e. after k = log log n steps.
The outer loop runs with i = 1, 2, 4, 8, and the inner loop runs i times each: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 (in general Θ(n)).
The outer loop runs with i = 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 (5 times), and the inner loop runs n = 16 times each: 5 × 16 = 80. In general n(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1) = Θ(n log n).

items.q: *(2 marks)* The solution of T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n is
items.w: n^(log₂ 2) = n and f(n) = n · log¹ n, so the extended case 2 (k = 1) gives Θ(n · log^(k+1) n) = Θ(n log² n).

items.q: *(2 marks)* A dynamic array starts with capacity 1. Whenever it is full and another element arrives, its capacity is doubled by copying all existing elements into a new array. The total number of element copies made while appending 16 elements one at a time is
items.w: Doubling happens when the 2nd, 3rd, 5th and 9th elements arrive, copying 1, 2, 4 and 8 elements: 15 copies in all. The cost per append is O(1) amortised.

items.q: *(1 mark)* If f(n) = O(g(n)) and g(n) = O(f(n)), then
o: nothing can be said about f and g
items.w: Each bounds the other from above, so each is within a constant factor of the other: f = Θ(g).

items.q: *(1 mark)* The maximum number of comparisons binary search makes on a sorted array of 1000 elements is
items.w: The worst case is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 = ⌊9.97⌋ + 1 = 10.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The number of inversions in the array 5, 2, 4, 1, 3 (pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j]) is
items.w: The inversions are (5,2), (5,4), (5,1), (5,3), (2,1), (4,1), (4,3): 7. Insertion sort performs exactly this many swaps.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Quick sort that always picks the first element as the pivot is run on an already sorted array of 10 distinct elements. The total number of key comparisons made in partitioning is
items.w: Each partition puts the pivot in place and leaves one subarray of size one less, so the comparisons are 9 + 8 + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 = 45.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The maximum number of comparisons merge sort makes to sort 8 elements is
items.w: Merging two lists of total size k needs at most k − 1 comparisons. T(2) = 1, T(4) = 2T(2) + 3 = 5, T(8) = 2T(4) + 7 = 17.

items.q: *(2 marks)* In the worst case, the number of comparisons needed to merge two sorted lists of 10 and 15 elements into one sorted list is
items.w: Each comparison outputs one element, and the last element needs no comparison: m + n − 1 = 24.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The minimum number of comparisons needed in the worst case to find both the maximum and the minimum of 100 distinct numbers is
items.w: Compare elements in pairs (50 comparisons), then find the maximum among the 50 winners (49) and the minimum among the 50 losers (49): 50 + 49 + 49 = 148 = ⌈3n/2⌉ − 2.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The minimum number of comparisons needed in the worst case to find the second largest of 16 distinct numbers is
items.w: Run a knockout tournament (15 comparisons). The second largest lost directly to the winner, and the winner played log₂ 16 = 4 matches, so another 4 − 1 = 3 comparisons among those 4 losers: 15 + 3 = 18 = n + ⌈log₂ n⌉ − 2.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The minimum number of comparisons that any comparison-based algorithm needs in the worst case to sort 5 distinct elements is at least
items.w: A decision tree must have at least 5! = 120 leaves, so its height is at least ⌈log₂ 120⌉ = 7 (2⁷ = 128).

items.q: *(2 marks)* Which of the following sorting algorithms is NOT stable?
items.w: Heap sort moves elements across long distances when it swaps the root with the last leaf, which can reorder equal keys. Bubble sort, insertion sort and merge sort preserve the order of equal elements.

items.q: *(2 marks)* n integers, each in the range 0 to n² − 1, are sorted using radix sort with base n (two digits). The running time is
items.w: Each integer has d = 2 digits in base n. Each pass is a counting sort taking Θ(n + base) = Θ(n), so two passes take Θ(n).

items.q: *(2 marks)* A hash table of size 10 uses chaining with h(k) = k mod 10. The keys 15, 25, 35, 12 and 22 are inserted. The length of the longest chain is
items.w: 15, 25 and 35 all hash to slot 5, giving a chain of length 3. 12 and 22 share slot 2 (length 2).

items.q: *(2 marks)* A table of size 7 uses h(k) = k mod 7 with linear probing. The keys 10, 17, 3 and 24 are inserted in this order. The slot in which 24 is stored is
items.w: 10 → slot 3. 17 maps to 3 (taken) → 4. 3 maps to 3 and 4 (taken) → 5. 24 maps to 3, 4, 5 (taken) → 6.

items.q: *(2 marks)* In an open-addressed hash table with uniform hashing and load factor α = 0.5, the expected number of probes in an unsuccessful search is about
items.w: The expected number of probes for an unsuccessful search is 1/(1 − α) = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A hash table with chaining has 500 slots and stores 2000 keys using a good hash function. The average length of a chain (the load factor) is
items.w: Load factor α = n/m = 2000 / 500 = 4 keys per chain on average, so an unsuccessful search examines about 4 keys.

items.q: *(1 mark)* Which of the following collision-resolution methods suffers from primary clustering?
items.w: With linear probing, runs of occupied slots grow longer because any key landing in a run extends it. Quadratic probing causes only milder secondary clustering, and double hashing and chaining avoid both.

items.q: *(2 marks)* In an open-addressed hash table, a key is deleted by simply marking its slot as empty. This can cause
o: searches for other keys that were probed past this slot to fail wrongly
items.w: A search stops at the first empty slot. If a later key was placed beyond the deleted slot, the search will now stop early and miss it. A tombstone marker avoids this.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Three keys are hashed independently and uniformly into a table of 10 slots. The probability that all three land in different slots is
items.w: The second key avoids 1 slot (9/10) and the third avoids 2 slots (8/10): 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.72.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Strassen's matrix multiplication replaces 8 recursive half-size multiplications by 7. Its running time on n × n matrices is
items.w: T(n) = 7T(n/2) + Θ(n²) and n^(log₂ 7) ≈ n^2.81 dominates n², so T(n) = Θ(n^(log₂ 7)) by case 1 of the master theorem.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Karatsuba's algorithm multiplies two n-digit numbers using 3 half-size multiplications and linear extra work. Its running time is
items.w: T(n) = 3T(n/2) + Θ(n), and n^(log₂ 3) ≈ n^1.585 beats n, so T(n) = Θ(n^(log₂ 3)).

items.q: *(2 marks)* The divide-and-conquer algorithm that finds the closest pair among n points in the plane takes
items.w: The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), because the combine step inspects only a strip of points near the dividing line in linear time. This gives Θ(n log n).

items.q: *(1 mark)* The recurrence for binary search is T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. Its solution is
items.w: n^(log₂ 1) = 1 matches f(n) = 1 (case 2), so T(n) = Θ(log n): the array is halved about log₂ n times.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Consider the activities with (start, finish) times (1,3), (2,5), (4,7), (6,9), (8,10) and (9,12). The maximum number of mutually compatible activities that can be scheduled on one resource is
items.w: Greedy by earliest finish picks (1,3), then (4,7) (the first starting at or after 3), then (8,10). The remaining (9,12) overlaps (8,10). Three activities is optimal.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Symbols with frequencies 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 are encoded with a Huffman code. The total cost Σ frequency × code length is
items.w: Merge 3 + 5 = 8; then 7 + 8 = 15; then 9 + 12 = 21; then 15 + 21 = 36. The cost is the sum of the merged weights: 8 + 15 + 21 + 36 = 80.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Symbols have the frequencies 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8. In an optimal Huffman code, the length of the longest codeword is
items.w: The merges are 1 + 1 = 2, 2 + 2 = 4, 3 + 4 = 7, 5 + 7 = 12 and 8 + 12 = 20. Each merge takes the previous result, so the tree is a chain, and the two rarest symbols sit at depth 5.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A knapsack has capacity 40, and items (value, weight) are (30, 5), (40, 10), (45, 15) and (60, 20). Items can be taken fractionally. The maximum total value is
items.w: The value/weight ratios are 6, 4, 3 and 3. Take the first three whole (weight 30, value 115), then 10 of the 20 units of the last item (value 30): 145.

items.q: *(1 mark)* Which of the following problems is NOT solved optimally by the greedy method of taking the highest value-to-weight ratio first?
items.w: In the 0/1 problem items cannot be split, so a high-ratio item can leave capacity unused that another combination would fill. (The other three have valid greedy solutions, though activity selection and Huffman use different rules.)

items.q: *(2 marks)* Five unit-time jobs have (profit, deadline): (50, 2), (10, 1), (20, 2), (30, 1) and (40, 3). Jobs are scheduled greedily by decreasing profit, each in the latest free slot not after its deadline. The maximum total profit is
items.w: 50 goes in slot 2, 40 in slot 3, 30 in slot 1. The jobs worth 20 (deadline 2) and 10 (deadline 1) find no free slot. Profit 50 + 40 + 30 = 120.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Files of sizes 2, 3, 5 and 7 are merged two at a time, and merging two files costs the sum of their sizes. The minimum total cost of merging all of them into one file is
items.w: Always merge the two smallest: 2 + 3 = 5 (cost 5); 5 + 5 = 10 (cost 10); 7 + 10 = 17 (cost 17). Total 5 + 10 + 17 = 32.

items.q: *(2 marks)* For coin denominations {1, 3, 4}, the amount 6 is paid using the greedy "largest coin first" rule. How many more coins does greedy use than the optimal solution?
items.w: Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) but the optimum is 3 + 3 (2 coins). The difference is 1.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The length of the longest common subsequence of ACGTTGCA and CTGACTA is
items.w: Filling the LCS table gives 5. One longest common subsequence is CTGCA: it appears in order in ACGTTGCA (A-C-G-T-T-G-C-A) and in CTGACTA, and the table shows nothing of length 6 exists.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The edit distance (minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions) between "algorithm" and "altruistic" is
items.w: The table computed by the standard recurrence gives 6.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Four matrices A1 (10×20), A2 (20×5), A3 (5×30) and A4 (30×8) are to be multiplied. The minimum number of scalar multiplications needed over all parenthesisations is
items.w: The matrix-chain dynamic programme with p = (10, 20, 5, 30, 8) gives 2600, achieved by (A1 A2)(A3 A4): A1A2 costs 10·20·5 = 1000, A3A4 costs 5·30·8 = 1200, and multiplying the 10×5 and 5×8 results costs 10·5·8 = 400. Other parenthesisations are costlier, for example ((A1 A2) A3) A4 costs 1000 + 1500 + 2400 = 4900.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The number of different ways of fully parenthesising the product of 6 matrices A1 A2 A3 A4 A5 A6 is
items.w: The number of parenthesisations of n matrices is the Catalan number C(n−1). For n = 6 it is C₅ = C(10, 5) / 6 = 42.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A 0/1 knapsack has capacity 40 and items (weight, value): (5, 30), (10, 40), (15, 45) and (20, 60). The maximum total value is
items.w: The best choice is weights 5 + 15 + 20 = 40 with value 30 + 45 + 60 = 135. (145 is only possible if the last item may be split.)

items.q: *(1 mark)* The standard dynamic-programming algorithm for the longest common subsequence of strings of lengths m and n has time complexity
items.w: The table has (m + 1)(n + 1) entries and each is filled in constant time from three neighbours: Θ(mn).

items.q: *(2 marks)* The length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of 3, 10, 2, 1, 20, 4, 6, 12 is
items.w: One longest subsequence is 2, 4, 6, 12 (another is 1, 4, 6, 12). Subsequences starting with 3 reach 3, 10, 20 (length 3) or 3, 4, 6, 12 (length 4).

items.q: *(2 marks)* In a 5 × 5 grid of cells, a token starts at the top-left cell and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down one cell at a time. The number of different paths is
items.w: Every path has 4 right-moves and 4 down-moves in some order: C(8, 4) = 70.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The number of ways to make a total of 10 using unlimited coins of values 1, 2 and 5 (the order of coins does not matter) is
items.w: Counting combinations with the dynamic programme ways[x] += ways[x − c] for each coin in turn gives 10 ways.

items.q: *(1 mark)* Dynamic programming is most appropriate for a problem when
o: it has optimal substructure and its recursive subproblems overlap
items.w: If subproblems overlap, plain recursion repeats the same work exponentially often, and a table (memoisation) removes the repetition. When subproblems are independent, divide and conquer is enough.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A weighted undirected graph on vertices A to F has edges AB = 4, AC = 2, BC = 1, BD = 5, CD = 8, CE = 10, DE = 2, DF = 6 and EF = 3. The weight of a minimum spanning tree is
items.w: Kruskal: add BC (1), AC (2), DE (2), EF (3). AB (4) would close a cycle A–B–C. Add BD (5), which joins {A, B, C} with {D, E, F}. Five edges, total 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 13.

items.q: *(1 mark)* If all the edge weights of a connected undirected graph are distinct, then its minimum spanning tree
items.w: With distinct weights the cut property picks a single lightest edge across every cut, so only one MST is possible. With ties, several MSTs of equal total weight can exist.

items.q: *(1 mark)* Prim's algorithm on a graph with V vertices, using an adjacency matrix and a simple array to find the minimum edge, runs in time
items.w: Each of the V iterations scans an array of V entries to pick the closest outside vertex and updates the neighbours, so V × V = O(V²). With a binary heap and adjacency lists it is O(E log V).

items.q: *(2 marks)* A directed graph has edges S→A (4), S→B (1), B→A (2), A→C (1) and B→C (5). The length of the shortest path from S to C is
items.w: Dijkstra: B = 1, then A = min(4, 1 + 2) = 3, then C = min(1 + 5, 3 + 1) = 4. The path is S → B → A → C.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Which of the following algorithms may give a wrong answer on a graph that has negative edge weights but no negative cycle?
items.w: Dijkstra finalises a vertex when it is first removed from the queue, assuming no later path can be shorter. A negative edge can break that assumption. Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall handle negative edges.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The Bellman–Ford algorithm runs on a graph with 7 vertices that has no negative cycle. After how many passes over all edges are the shortest-path distances from the source guaranteed to be final?
items.w: A shortest path has at most V − 1 = 6 edges, and pass k fixes all paths of k edges. So 6 passes are enough (a 7th pass is only used to detect negative cycles).

items.q: *(2 marks)* A depth-first search is run on a directed graph. The graph contains a directed cycle if and only if the DFS finds
items.w: A back edge points from a vertex to one of its ancestors in the DFS tree, closing a cycle. Conversely, every directed cycle forces a back edge.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The directed graph with edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, 3→4, 4→5 and 5→4 has how many strongly connected components?
items.w: Vertices 1, 2 and 3 form a cycle, so they form one component. Vertices 4 and 5 form a cycle, so they form another. The edge 3→4 goes only one way, so the two components are separate.

items.q: *(1 mark)* The Floyd–Warshall algorithm on a graph with 100 vertices performs about how many innermost relaxation steps?
items.w: The algorithm has three nested loops over the vertices, so V³ = 100³ = 10⁶ steps.

blocks.text: #### Cheat sheet: Algorithms on one page

items.question: Solve T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n² and say which case of the master theorem applies.
items.answer: n^(log₂ 4) = n² matches f(n) = n² exactly (case 2 with k = 0), so T(n) = Θ(n² log n).

items.question: Why does the greedy "largest ratio first" rule fail for 0/1 knapsack but work for fractional knapsack?
items.answer: In the fractional version leftover capacity is filled with part of an item, so the rule never wastes capacity. In 0/1 an item cannot be split, so a high-ratio item can leave unused space that a different combination would fill. Example: capacity 40 with the four items of the worked example gives greedy 115 but optimum 135.

items.question: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm give wrong answers on negative edges?
items.answer: It treats the distance of a popped vertex as final. A negative edge discovered later could still lower that distance, but Dijkstra never revisits it.

items.question: What is the amortised cost of an append to a dynamic array that doubles when full?
items.answer: Over n appends the total copying is at most 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n/2 < n, so the total work is below 2n and each append costs O(1) amortised, even though a single append can cost Θ(n).
